title: Probability as Counting
coreInsight: Probability measures an event relative to a complete probability model; for equally likely discrete outcomes, it is the fraction of the sample space that is favorable.
targetLearnerRealization: Probability compares a target event with a complete sample space; favorable/total works only when the elementary outcomes are equally likely.
learningObjectives: Build a complete sample space of equally likely elementary outcomes.
Represent an event as a subset of that sample space and calculate its probability as favorable outcomes divided by total outcomes.
Distinguish equally likely elementary outcomes from summarized categories that may have different likelihoods.

continuity.openingCallback: Reuse C2's complete outcome grid for two coin tosses, then mark the leaves that make an event happen.
closingSeeds: A probability denominator describes the outcomes still possible in the current sample space.
When an object is removed without replacement, the sample space for the next draw changes.

misconceptionTargets.misconception: All outcomes that are easy to list are equally likely.
The sample space can be incomplete.
Probability is just the number of favorable outcomes.
The numerator and denominator may refer to different universes.

beats.purpose: Briefly reactivate C2's completeness audit and immediately turn the completed list toward chance.
beats.expectedRealization: Two successive fair coin tosses have four complete, distinct outcomes.
beats.transitionIn: Last time, a list was trustworthy only when every finished path appeared once. Rebuild one tiny list we can audit completely.
beats.prompt: A fair coin is tossed twice. How many complete outcomes belong in the grid?

visual.ariaLabel: Heads or tails on each of two successive fair coin tosses

response.feedback: Count complete two-toss records, not the two labels on a coin.

beats.correctFeedback: Yes—HH, HT, TH, and TT complete the grid.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Give each possible first toss both possible second-toss endings.

visual.ariaLabel: Complete two by two outcome grid HH, HT, TH, TT

steps.title: Finish every branch
steps.body: After either first toss, the second toss can be H or T.

resolution.takeaway: The four cells are the complete two-toss outcomes, and each is equally likely for a fair coin.

beats.purpose: Have the learner locate an event inside a complete outcome space before giving formal vocabulary.
beats.expectedRealization: Exactly one head occurs in two of the four equally likely cells, HT and TH.
beats.transitionIn: Keep all four cells. Now ask a question about which of those finished outcomes count as a success.
beats.prompt: How many cells show exactly one head?

visual.ariaLabel: Neutral two-toss outcome grid before any successful cells are marked

response.feedback: Inspect all four complete records and count the ones containing one H.

beats.correctFeedback: Right—HT and TH are the two successes.
beats.incorrectFeedback: HH has two heads and TT has none; check the other two cells.

visual.ariaLabel: Outcome grid with HT and TH marked as the outcomes having exactly one head

steps.title: Test the same condition everywhere
steps.body: HT and TH each contain exactly one H; HH and TT do not.

resolution.takeaway: A chance question selects some outcomes from the complete set.

beats.purpose: Elicit the favorable-to-total ratio and repair favorable-count-only thinking.
beats.expectedRealization: The two successful cells must be compared with all four equally likely cells, giving 2/4.
beats.transitionIn: Two successes alone do not say how likely the event is. Two successes out of four possibilities is different from two out of twenty.
beats.prompt: Which fraction measures the chance of getting exactly one head?

visual.ariaLabel: Four equally likely outcomes with two successful outcomes marked

options.text: 2/4, because two of the four equally likely outcomes succeed
1/2, because a coin has two face labels

feedback.count: A count needs a complete total for comparison.
feedback.ratio: Exactly—the numerator and denominator refer to the same four-cell grid.
feedback.labels: The experiment has two tosses, so its elementary outcomes are the four complete records.

beats.correctFeedback: Exactly—2 favorable outcomes out of 4 total outcomes.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Use the marked cells for the numerator and every cell in that same grid for the denominator.

steps.title: Count the marked part
steps.body: There are two outcomes with exactly one head.

steps.title: Compare with the whole grid
steps.body: The complete grid contains four equally likely outcomes.

resolution.takeaway: The numerator and denominator must describe the same experiment and the same complete outcome space.

beats.purpose: Expose the mistake of treating summarized outcome categories as equally likely.
beats.expectedRealization: The labels 0 heads, 1 head, and 2 heads hide different numbers of equally likely elementary outcomes.
beats.transitionIn: The four-cell grid can be summarized with just three labels: 0 heads, 1 head, or 2 heads. A shorter list can hide unequal weights.
beats.prompt: For two fair tosses, are the three head-count labels equally likely?

visual.ariaLabel: Three possible summarized head-count labels with no probabilities shown

options.text: Yes. There are three labels, so each has chance 1/3.
No. One head is more likely than either zero heads or two heads.
No. Zero heads and two heads are more likely than one head.

feedback.equal: Labels are categories, not necessarily equally likely elementary outcomes. Reopen the four-cell grid.
feedback.one-more: Yes. The one-head category contains two cells; each extreme contains one.
feedback.extremes: The two mixed outcomes HT and TH both belong to the one-head category.

beats.correctFeedback: Right—the three category names do not carry equal weight.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Sort HH, HT, TH, and TT by head count, then compare the group sizes.

visual.ariaLabel: Four elementary outcomes sorted into head-count categories of sizes one, two, and one

steps.title: Look beneath each label
steps.body: The three categories contain 1, 2, and 1 equally likely cells.

steps.title: Check coverage and overlap
steps.body: Every one of HH, HT, TH, and TT appears in exactly one category, so the grouping is complete and non-overlapping.

resolution.takeaway: Easy-to-name categories are not automatically equally likely. Count the equally likely elementary outcomes inside them.

beats.purpose: Attach formal probability language to the learner's favorable-part versus complete-whole discovery.
beats.expectedRealization: For equally likely elementary outcomes, an event's probability is favorable outcomes divided by all outcomes in the sample space.
beats.transitionIn: You already used the idea: build the complete equally likely grid, mark the cells that satisfy the question, and compare marked cells with all cells. Now name the pieces.
beats.name: Sample space, event, and probability
beats.conciseDefinition: The sample space is the complete set of possible elementary outcomes. An event is the subset that satisfies the question.
beats.formalization: When all elementary outcomes are equally likely, P(event) = (number of favorable outcomes)/(number of outcomes in the sample space).
beats.memoryHook: Build the whole, mark the event, then compare part to whole.

beats.purpose: Test equal-likelihood at the elementary-section level when visible labels repeat.
beats.expectedRealization: A fair four-section spinner has four equally likely sections even when only three different letters appear.
beats.transitionIn: The formula is short, but it carries a condition: the things in the denominator must be equally likely. Repeated labels make that condition visible.
beats.prompt: A fair spinner has four equal sections labeled A, A, B, C. What is the probability of landing on A?

visual.ariaLabel: Four equal spinner sections labeled A, A, B, and C with no successful sections marked

options.text: 1/3, because A, B, and C are the three labels
2/4 = 1/2, because two of the four equal sections say A

feedback.third: The three letter categories do not have equal numbers of sections.
feedback.half: Exactly. The equal sections—not the distinct labels—are the elementary outcomes.
feedback.two: Two is the favorable count; compare it with all four equal sections.

beats.correctFeedback: Yes—two favorable equal sections out of four total sections.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Use the four physical sections as the equally likely outcomes.

visual.ariaLabel: Four equal spinner sections with both A sections marked as favorable

steps.title: Choose the elementary outcomes
steps.body: The four equal physical sections are equally likely. The letter categories A, B, and C are not.

resolution.takeaway: Equal geometry gives equal likelihood to sections; repeated labels combine sections into a larger event.

beats.purpose: Apply the complete-space and favorable-subset method to a fresh two-coin event with a worked visual resolution.
beats.expectedRealization: At least one head includes three of the four equally likely two-coin outcomes.
beats.transitionIn: Use the full routine on the familiar four-cell model, but change the event being marked.
beats.transitionOut: The event changed from exactly one head to at least one head, while the complete four-cell denominator stayed fixed.
beats.whyNow: The learner has discovered and named the method and can now coordinate an inclusive event with the unchanged sample space.
beats.entryBridge: List both coins in order, then mark every record except the one with no heads.
beats.exitBridge: HH, HT, and TH are three favorable cells in the same complete four-cell grid.
beats.reusedRepresentation: The discovery grid is reused with a new event marked.
learnerPrompts: What are the four equally likely elementary outcomes?
Which outcomes contain at least one H?
Do the favorable count and total count refer to the same grid?
beats.correctFeedback: Correct—three of the four equally likely outcomes contain at least one head.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Write HH, HT, TH, TT, then remove only the outcome with zero heads.

visual.ariaLabel: Complete two-coin grid with HH, HT, and TH marked for at least one head

steps.title: Build the whole
steps.body: Two ordered coin results give HH, HT, TH, and TT, each with probability 1/4.

steps.title: Mark the event
steps.body: At least one head includes HH, HT, and TH. Only TT fails.

steps.title: Another way
steps.body: It is shorter to subtract the one all-tails outcome from the whole.

resolution.takeaway: An event may collect several elementary outcomes; its probability is their share of the complete equally likely space.

beats.purpose: Transfer from one two-coin grid to an asymmetric joint sample space while confronting unequal head-count categories.
beats.expectedRealization: Keiko's two outcomes pair with Ephraim's four outcomes to make eight equally likely joint outcomes, three of which have matching head counts.
beats.transitionIn: Now the two people do not toss the same number of coins. Head-count labels become even more tempting, so return to complete elementary outcomes.
beats.transitionOut: The three matching leaves mattered only relative to all eight equally likely joint leaves.
beats.whyNow: The learner can build and mark a small equal-likelihood space; this approved problem now tests whether that reasoning survives unequal numbers of coins and summarized head-count categories.
beats.entryBridge: Pair each Keiko result with every ordered two-penny result for Ephraim before comparing head counts.
beats.exitBridge: Matching on one head contributes two leaves, and matching on zero heads contributes one more; both cases belong in the event.
beats.reusedRepresentation: The two-coin outcome grid expands into a joint tree of equally likely leaves with matching leaves colored.
learnerPrompts: What are the eight equally likely joint outcomes?
Are the possible head counts themselves equally likely?
Which leaves match when Keiko has zero heads, and which match when she has one head?
beats.correctFeedback: Yes—three of the eight equally likely joint outcomes have matching head counts.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Do not stop with Keiko's one-head case. Open her tails branch and check the zero-head match too.

steps.title: Build all joint leaves
steps.body: Keiko has 2 outcomes and Ephraim has 4 ordered outcomes, so pairing them creates 8 equally likely joint outcomes.

steps.title: Mark both matching cases
steps.body: Keiko's T matches Ephraim's TT at zero heads. Keiko's H matches Ephraim's HT and TH at one head.

steps.title: Compare event with sample space
steps.body: Three of the eight equally likely leaves match.

resolution.takeaway: Count equally likely complete outcomes, not head-count labels, and include every disjoint way the event can happen.

beats.purpose: Check near transfer to repeated labels on equally sized spinner sections.
beats.expectedRealization: Three red sections among six equal sections give probability 3/6=1/2.
beats.transitionIn: Leave coins behind. The representation changes, but the denominator still comes from equally likely elementary outcomes.
beats.transitionOut: Distinct color names were not the denominator; the six equal sections were.
beats.whyNow: A near-transfer item checks the equal-section interpretation without the two-stage coin structure.
beats.entryBridge: Treat each equal section as one elementary outcome even when a color repeats.
beats.exitBridge: The three red sections form one event inside the six-section sample space.
beats.reusedRepresentation: The labeled-spinner model returns with a different number of equal sections.
learnerPrompts: What are the equally likely outcomes?
How many of those outcomes are red?
beats.correctFeedback: Correct—3 of 6 equal sections are red, so the probability is 1/2.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Count physical sections, not distinct color names.

visual.ariaLabel: Six equal spinner sections with three red sections marked

steps.body: Three of the six equally likely sections are red.

resolution.takeaway: Repeated labels combine elementary outcomes; they do not reduce the denominator to the number of distinct labels.

beats.purpose: Check near transfer on a different event in the familiar two-coin sample space.
beats.expectedRealization: The matching outcomes HH and TT occupy two of four equally likely cells.
beats.transitionIn: Return once to the four-cell coin grid, but let the event collect the two matching extremes.
beats.transitionOut: A verbal event became a precise subset: HH and TT, two cells out of four.
beats.whyNow: This verifies that the learner can define a new event without changing a familiar sample space.
beats.entryBridge: List the ordered results, then mark those whose two faces agree.
beats.exitBridge: Both matching outcomes are included, and neither mixed outcome is.
beats.reusedRepresentation: The original four-cell coin grid is reused for a matching event.
learnerPrompts: Which two outcomes have matching faces?
How many total equally likely outcomes remain in the grid?
beats.correctFeedback: Correct—HH and TT are 2 of the 4 equally likely outcomes.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Matching means both H or both T; keep all four outcomes in the denominator.

visual.ariaLabel: Four two-coin outcomes with HH and TT marked as matching

steps.body: HH and TT match; HT and TH do not.

resolution.takeaway: Changing the event changes the numerator, not the complete sample space.

beats.purpose: Transfer the method to a one-stage numerical sample space and enforce a shared numerator and denominator universe.
beats.expectedRealization: Among cards 1 through 8, only 3 and 6 are multiples of 3, giving 2/8=1/4.
beats.transitionIn: Coins and spinners supplied visible cells. A numbered set can serve as the same kind of complete space.
beats.transitionOut: The favorable cards and total cards came from the same set 1 through 8.
beats.whyNow: A mixed representation checks whether the learner can construct the event from a numerical property.
beats.entryBridge: Write the full card set first, then test divisibility by 3 one card at a time.
beats.exitBridge: Two favorable cards out of the same eight-card universe simplify to one fourth.
beats.reusedRepresentation: The outcome grid becomes a lineup of equally likely numbered cards.
learnerPrompts: What is the complete set of cards?
beats.correctFeedback: Correct—3 and 6 are the two favorable cards among eight.
beats.incorrectFeedback: List 1 through 8, then mark only numbers divisible by 3 with no remainder.

visual.ariaLabel: Eight numbered cards with 3 and 6 marked as multiples of 3

steps.body: The complete sample space is 1 through 8. Its favorable subset is {3, 6}.

resolution.takeaway: Build the denominator and numerator from the same universe.

beats.purpose: Require a complete product sample space before testing a sum condition.
beats.expectedRealization: A two-section and three-section fair spinner create six equally likely ordered pairs, three with an even sum.
beats.transitionIn: Now the complete space is not handed to you. Build it from two successive choices, just as in C1 and C2, then mark the event.
beats.transitionOut: The 2-by-3 grid proved both completeness and equal weighting before any favorable count was used.
beats.whyNow: This mixed item combines prior product-space construction with the new favorable-to-total comparison.
beats.entryBridge: Pair every result from the 1-2 spinner with every result from the 1-2-3 spinner.
beats.exitBridge: Three even-sum cells among six equally likely cells give one half.
beats.reusedRepresentation: C1's rectangular choice grid becomes a probability sample space.
learnerPrompts: How many ordered pairs fill the complete grid?
Which pairs have an even sum?
beats.correctFeedback: Correct—three of the six equally likely pairs have an even sum.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Make both rows of the 2-by-3 grid, then check each sum's parity.

visual.ariaLabel: Two by three spinner outcome grid with the three even-sum pairs marked

steps.title: Complete the grid
steps.body: Two first-spinner results pair with three second-spinner results.

steps.title: Mark even sums
steps.body: The pairs (1,1), (1,3), and (2,2) have even sums.

resolution.takeaway: First certify the sample space; then count the event inside it.

beats.purpose: Challenge the learner to count a complement in a twelve-outcome product space without losing the complete denominator.
beats.expectedRealization: A product is odd only when both factors are odd, so four of twelve pairs are odd and eight are favorable.
beats.transitionIn: For the final challenge, the grid has twelve cells. A useful opposite event can shorten the marking without changing the denominator.
beats.transitionOut: Counting the four odd-product exceptions exposed all eight favorable cells without listing them one by one.
beats.whyNow: The challenge preserves the primary complete-space method while rewarding an elegant complement count grounded in parity.
beats.entryBridge: Build the 3-by-4 space, then ask when a product fails to be even.
beats.exitBridge: The four odd-odd pairs are the complete complement, leaving eight of twelve pairs favorable.
beats.reusedRepresentation: The rectangular spinner grid scales up and is audited through its complement.
learnerPrompts: How many equally likely ordered pairs are there?
Exactly when is a product odd?
How many cells remain for an even product?
beats.correctFeedback: Correct—8 of the 12 equally likely pairs have an even product, so the probability is 2/3.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Count odd products first: both spinner results must be odd.

visual.ariaLabel: Three by four outcome grid showing eight even products and four odd products

steps.title: Keep the complete denominator
steps.body: The two fair spinners make 3×4=12 equally likely ordered pairs.

steps.title: Count the opposite event
steps.body: A product is odd only for odd-odd pairs. There are 2 odd choices on each spinner, so 2×2=4 odd-product pairs.

steps.title: Return to the target event
steps.body: The remaining eight pairs have even products.

resolution.takeaway: A complement can simplify the favorable count, but both counts still live inside the same complete sample space.

beats.purpose: Consolidate the full probability-as-counting routine and its equal-likelihood condition before looking forward.
beats.expectedRealization: A valid favorable-over-total calculation requires a complete nonduplicated space, equally likely elementary outcomes, and one shared universe.
beats.transitionIn: Coins, cards, and spinners all used the same audit. Gather the checks before the sample space begins to change.
beats.prompt: Which checks make favorable/total a valid probability calculation here? Select all four.

options.text: The sample space contains every possible elementary outcome.
Each elementary outcome is counted exactly once.
The elementary outcomes in the denominator are equally likely.
The favorable outcomes are a subset of that same sample space.
Every easy-to-name category gets one equal share.

response.feedback: Audit the whole space, its weights, and the relationship between the event and that whole.

beats.correctFeedback: Exactly—complete, nonduplicated, equally likely, and one shared universe.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Named categories may contain different numbers of elementary outcomes; keep the four structural checks.

groups.label: 3. Mark the event
choices: Favorable outcomes come from that whole

steps.body: A complete, nonduplicated list establishes the denominator.
Equal likelihood makes a simple count ratio valid.
The event selects favorable outcomes from that exact denominator.

resolution.takeaway: Build the whole, check equal likelihood, mark the event, and compare part to that same whole.

beats.purpose: Create the precise unresolved question that leads to P2 after P1 has been consolidated.
beats.expectedRealization: If an outcome is removed before a second draw, the second sample space may have a different total and composition.
beats.transitionIn: So far, every trial used a fixed complete space. Keep the audit, but disturb the space itself.
beats.prompt: A bag holds three tiles. You draw one and do not put it back. Before the second draw, what happened to the denominator—and could the favorable part have changed too?
beats.takeaway: Next, we will let an earlier outcome change the sample space for what happens afterward.

notes: Draft foundation lesson authored with the repository-local mathinking-lesson Skill and the compact P1 context packet.
The opening reactivates C2's completeness audit only long enough to transform its two-coin grid into a probability model.
The approved AMC 8 2000 Problem 21 appears in its guided role after equal likelihood and summarized-category traps have been discovered.
All declarative visuals reuse existing generic primitives; the mapped penny-match-tree animation is reused without renderer changes.
Generated questions were independently enumerated and checked with complementary arithmetic or parity arguments.
